Description

Rocky Mountain Conservancy is excited to offer two seasonal environmental education fellowships that give current students and recent college graduates the opportunity to serve in a national park while exploring careers in environmental education and the nonprofit sector. Each fellowship is unique and tailored to the individual’s skills, interests, and career goals. This is your chance to live and learn in Rocky Mountain National Park, while supporting the Conservancy's efforts in education, stewardship, and conservation!  


2027 Fellowship dates: April 14th, 2027 - October 20th, 2027


First review of applications: December 1, 2026


These fellowships are designed for highly motivated individuals passionate about outreach and education. Successful fellows thrive in a self-directed environment, where there is a balance between Conservancy-assigned and fellow-selected projects. Each fellowship includes: 

On-the-job training and experience in a variety of environmental education programs and settings 
Opportunities to develop and lead programs individually and in partnership with both Rocky Mountain Conservancy (RMC) and Rocky Mountain National Park (RMNP) teams 
Housing and utilities are provided at no cost along with a stipend for living expenses 
Professional development and networking opportunities with park and nonprofit staff 

As a fellow, you will have the opportunity to build real-world experience in both the nonprofit and public sectors. Our fellowship will help you develop: 

A deep understanding of the Conservancy’s work and partnerships 
Knowledge of the region’s natural and cultural history 
Skills in program planning and delivery, participant communication, and outreach 
A professional portfolio of education and outreach work products 

Required Skills: 

Dedication to environmental and outdoor education, with the ability to lead programs for children, teens, and adults 
Adept communication skills, both written and spoken, for diverse audiences and using various media 
Strong problem-solving skills, and the ability to organize ideas and information quickly 
Demonstrated ability to independently manage long-term projects and complete assignments on time 
Desire and ability to work both collaboratively and independently 
Computer experience with Canva and the Microsoft Office suite, including Word and Outlook, preferred 
Enthusiasm, a warm disposition, and the ability to handle the stresses of working outdoors with diverse groups of program participants 

Responsibilities: 

Develop and lead interactive outdoor programs (i.e. pop-up table talks, and educational bus tours) for diverse audiences, including families, youth, and adults 
Support expert-led Field Institute programs
Assist with development, planning, and implementation for a range of Conservancy programs 
Support RMNP education and interpretation programs, such as school field trips and Jr. Ranger programs 
Create outreach and promotional materials for Conservancy programs 
Establish and maintain positive working relationships with RMNP staff and volunteers, as well as with other Conservancy partners, program participants, and community members 
Assist Conservancy and park staff with outreach events 
Drive and/or ride in Conservancy-owned vehicles, including the Conservancy’s 15-passenger buses 
Each position averages 30-40 hours per week, with schedules that vary throughout the fellowship. A full 6-month commitment is required.  

Fellows are provided with housing (including all utilities) for the duration of their fellowship. Shared housing units are located near Conservancy headquarters in Estes Park, CO, in units operated by Rocky Mountain National Park. Fellows also receive a living stipend of $450/week (paid as $900 every two weeks). Fellows must be eligible to work in the USA and must pass a background check. 


It is recommended that the candidate be actively pursuing or have recently completed a degree program in environmental education, general education, communication, outdoor recreation/tourism, natural resource management, or similar. In addition, experience volunteering or working with nonprofit organizations and an interest in public outreach and conservation is desired. 


Visit us online to learn more: https://rmconservancy.org/work-with-us/environmental-education-fellowships/

How to Apply
To apply, email your resume, cover letter, and at least three professional references (including phone numbers and
email addresses) to [email removed] In the subject line, specify whether you’re applying for the Outdoor Education Fellowship or the Environmental Education Fellowship.

Description
The Biology Department at East Tennessee State University (ETSU) is seeking a motivated masters student starting fall 2027 to join Dr. Ryan Stephens' lab (https://ryanbstephens.wordpress.com). The Stephens’ lab focuses on understanding ecological interactions and community dynamics with a strong focus on trophic ecology of mammals and their consumption and dispersal of fungal spores and seeds. Graduate students will have the opportunity to work on projects involving both field research and lab-based studies, contributing to our understanding of ecological interactions and the functional roles that small mammals play in forested ecosystems. There is room for project development depending on the student’s interest with main research foci including 1) truffle-mammal interactions and the dispersal of fungal spores, 2) seed selection and dispersal by small mammals, and 3) trophic niche dynamics of small mammals.
 Position Requirements:
A bachelor’s degree in biology, ecology, environmental science, or a related field.
Previous research experience in ecology, natural resources, biology, or a related discipline is preferred.
·       Experience with field data collection, especially small mammal live trapping or taking forest compositional measurements is preferred but not required.
A valid US drivers license (or the ability to get one).
 Opportunities and Support:
The position is based at ETSU in Johnson City Tennessee and is available beginning August 2027. The ideal candidate will be able to start field data collection in May of 2027. Field work will take place in the Blue Ridge Mountains of East Tennessee. The Masters student will have support for 2 years including a tuition waver and stipend ($12,200) along with summer salary guaranteed in 2027.
 To apply, please email ([email removed]) your CV, statement of research interests (2 pages max), and contact information for three references. Include “Graduate student application” along with your last name in the email title. Review of applications will begin immediately and continue until the position is filled. To receive full consideration please apply before November 1, 2026. Please refer to https://www.etsu.edu/cas/biology/academics/ms_bio.php for information about the Biology M.S. program.

Description
*Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A postdoctoral research opportunity focused on the development of novel detection methods for foodborne pathogenic bacteria is available at the USDA, Agricultural Research Service, Eastern Regional Research Center, Characterization and Interventions for Foodborne Pathogens (CIFP) Research Unit in Wyndmoor, Pennsylvania.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: The mission of the CIFP research unit is to investigate multiple areas of safety-related problems associated with contamination of food by bacterial pathogens and includes: stress response, evolution/mutation, biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, intervention techniques, and rapid detection & identification. The research project in this subgroup focuses on the stress responses for specific foodborne pathogenic bacteria (e.g., Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes). Analysis is typically complicated by the complex nature of food matrices and the frequent need to develop virulence assays using different mammalian cell lines.

During the appointment, you will assist in research and development focused on one or more advanced areas of interest (e.g., molecular microbiology and biochemistry). This research will complement your academic education with the application of:

BSL2 pathogen handling
Genome sequencing, transcriptomics
Bioinformatic analysis, Computational biology
Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Learn about food-safety research focused on bacterial contamination and foodborne pathogens.
Develop knowledge of stress-response mechanisms in pathogens such as Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, Salmonella, and Listeria monocytogenes.
Gain experience investigating pathogen evolution and mutation, biofilm formation, antimicrobial resistance, and virulence.
Learn how food-matrix complexity affects the detection, characterization, and analysis of foodborne bacteria.
Build skills in developing and conducting virulence assays using mammalian cell lines.
Strengthen laboratory research, experimental-design, and data-analysis skills relevant to microbial food-safety studies.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Andrew Gehring ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: December 1, 2026. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Participant Stipend: The participant will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience. The anticipated stipend is $6,857/mo with an allowance of $691.68/mo for health insurance. 

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should have received or be currently pursuing a doctoral degree in the one of the relevant fields.

Preferred skills:

Sterile technique
Knowledge of polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
DNA/RNA isolation
Basic molecular techniques

Description
The Smith BIRDS Lab (https://smithbirdslab.com/) is recruiting graduate students (MS or PhD) for fall 2027 or spring 2028. The lab has a wide range of research interests but focuses its core on farming for people and nature. Research on co-managing farmlands for avian conservation and ecosystem service provisioning is a large portion of the lab’s efforts. We currently seek students to work on projects related to (1) ecosystem services and disservices resulting from songbird nestbox use, (2) conservation outcomes of using songbird nestboxes on farms, and (3) optimal prairie strip implementation and design for birds and ecosystem services. While birds are a large interest of the lab, we also work with insects, particularly in the context of integrated pest management. Current projects focus on insect pest control services provided by birds and food safety externalities resulting from birds, and these lines of work are priorities to continue. We also are pursing lines of work related to avian reproductive success and parasite burden.

Applicants must have graduated with a bachelor’s degree in ecology or related field by June 2027. The ideal applicant would be self-motivated, driven, and a good community member, with prior experience conducting field work, analyzing data, and leading their own research project. If interested in applying, please fill out this Google Form in lieu of an email submission. Applications should be submitted by November 9th for full consideration. I will reach out to a subset of candidates to conduct follow-up interviews over Zoom. One to two applicants will be encouraged to apply for graduate admissions by mid-December.

Description
 Description 

The Holmes lab at Southern Illinois University is recruiting a PhD student for a fully funded, 5-year research assistantship. Application deadline is December 30. Salary is $25,700 per year. The research should focus on the impacts of roads on natural systems in the eastern hardwood forest, ideally with the possibility of improving conservation practices for state and federal threatened and endangered species. Contact Iris Holmes ([email removed]) for more information. 

Duties 

The student will conduct sampling for threatened and endangered bats at new construction sites (approximately 5-10 per year). Sampling will involve laying out tarps to collect fecal samples, preserving samples in the field, extracting DNA from the samples in the lab, and using Sanger sequencing to barcode the samples to identify bat species. A report on species IDs must be completed within 15 days of sample collection. 

Research focus 

In addition to bat monitoring, the student will develop a research program as part of the new Roadside Ecology Center at SIU. The taxon focus is flexible, but the research should apply to conservation of threatened and endangered species or to conservation of Illinois habitats. Possible research areas could include (but are not limited to) validating eDNA methods for detection of vertebrates or invertebrates from water samples, using eDNA methods to study connectivity in aquatic systems, developing analytical methods to account for imperfect detection in metapopulation or niche models, quantifying road impacts on animal diets, or determining the impact of construction- or road-related stressors on animal microbiomes or parasite infection rates. 

Desired qualifications 

Bachelor’s degree in biology or a related field 

Master’s degree or 1 or more years of work experience 

Experience with molecular lab work and/or field work 

Interest in landscape management or conservation policy

The Gilbert Lab at Oklahoma State University is recruiting a MS student, to start in January 2027, for a project intended to provide updated information on wading bird breeding colonies in Oklahoma, with a focus on Snowy Egrets and Little Blue Herons (both considered Species of Greatest Conservation Need in Oklahoma). The project is funded by the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation, and the  MS position is fully funded with a tuition waiver. The student will be funded on an RA during the spring semesters and summers and on a TA in the Department of Biology during the fall semesters. 

The student is expected to provide the following deliverables as part of the project: 1) canvass stakeholders to collate community knowledge about colony locations, 2) conduct two field seasons (roughly April through July) to search for and monitor colonies across the state of Oklahoma (mostly land-based surveys but with the possibility of kayak surveys for difficult-to-access areas), and 3) conduct analyses to quantify landscape characteristics influencing the presence, abundance, species composition, and stability of colonies. 

Qualifications:
BS in Biology, Wildlife, or related field
Excellent writing and communication skills
Experience conducting fieldwork under challenging conditions
Experience using R
Strong background in bird identification and ecology

Application instructions
Submit, as a single PDF, a brief (1 page maximum) cover letter describing your interest and qualification for the position and a current CV to [email removed] with the subject line “Heron MS position”. The deadline to apply is 31 October 2026. Applications will be reviewed 11/2-11/3 and Zoom interviews will be conducted 11/4-11/11.

Description
The Vennum Lab at Boise State University seeks a motivated graduate student to join the M.S. in Raptor Biology program and contribute to the Butte Valley Raptor Research Project, a long-term research and monitoring effort on Swainson's Hawks (Buteo swainsoni) in northern California.
 
For decades, this project has tracked known-age individuals through mark-resight and annual nest monitoring, building a multi-faceted, long-term dataset on reproductive success and demography. This foundation supports questions about life-history evolution and the conservation of this long-distance migrant. We are also working to expand the program with developing research on nestling physiology and telemetry-based movement data to examine how hawks use agricultural landscapes. Together, this growing dataset and its planned expansion open the door to interdisciplinary thesis questions spanning demography, life history, physiology, and movement ecology.
 
The student's thesis question will be developed collaboratively, drawing on the project's existing data and research directions while leaving room for the student's own interests and ideas. Expectations for data use and authorship will be outlined in a lab mentoring agreement.
 
The M.S. program begins in Fall 2027. There may be an opportunity to begin graduate research and on-site fieldwork earlier, around April 2027.
 Funding
This position is supported by a Teaching Assistantship, which includes:
 Tuition 
Healthcare benefits
$22,000 starting annual stipend

The Raptor Research Center (RRC) at Boise State has supported graduate education, research and technical assistance to researchers since 1987. Learn more about the RRC here website.
 Project Description
The position is part of the Butte Valley Raptor Research Project, a long-term effort studying raptor ecology, movement, and habitat use in northern California. The project combines field surveys, nest monitoring, banding, and habitat data collection to support conservation and management on working landscapes.

The student’s primary field duties will include searching for and monitoring nests, resighting color-banded birds, and banding nestlings. Under appropriate supervision and permits, the student may also have opportunities to climb trees and gain experience handling and banding multiple raptor species. A field vehicle and fuel are provided for project work.

Fieldwork is based in Macdoel, California, in the Butte Valley region. This rural, high-elevation basin includes grasslands, agricultural fields, and views of the surrounding mountains. Students should be comfortable living in a remote area with limited urban amenities. Because much of this work takes place on both public and private lands, the student will build working relationships with landowners and represent the project professionally. 

The student will work with a collaborative team from Boise State University, the SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry, and Avian Behavior Conservancy. The student will have opportunities to present at scientific conferences and publish their thesis research. 

Qualifications
Applicants do not need to have experience in all of these areas to apply. We are particularly interested in students who are excited to learn new approaches, develop their skills through graduate research, and can work well with project collaborators. We especially encourage applications from first-generation college students and people from groups underrepresented in wildlife biology. 
 
Required Qualifications
 Bachelor’s degree in biology, wildlife, ecology, or a related field, completed before the April 2027 start date.
Strong interest in avian ecology, population ecology, and/or demography
Strong organizational skills and attention to detail
Ability to work both independently and collaboratively in a research team
Ability to work outdoors for extended periods in variable weather conditions, including heat, dust, and sun exposure. This position requires regular fieldwork in remote and rugged environments.
A valid driver’s license

Preferred Qualifications

Experience with statistical data analysis or coding (e.g., R, Python, JavaScript)
Strong written and oral communication skills
Enthusiasm for interdisciplinary research bridging demography, physiology, and conservation
A positive attitude and commitment to contributing to a respectful, inclusive, and collaborative lab environment

Interested candidates should send the following materials to Dr. Chris Vennum at chrisvennum [at] boisestate.edu by November 13th, 2026:
 Cover Letter (1 page) – Describe your research interests, relevant experience and skills (see required and preferred qualifications), and why you are interested in this project and joining the Raptor Research Center at Boise State University.
Curriculum Vitae (CV) – Please include your GPA, relevant research or field experience, and contact information for three references.
 Submit all application materials in a single PDF file named:  LastName_FirstName_2026_SWHA_MS.pdf  

Questions about the position or project are welcomed by email.
Contact
Chris Vennum
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Assistant Professor of Biology - Tenure Track

The University of Central Missouri’s Biology Program is seeking applicants for a tenure-track position of Assistant Professor of Biology to begin in Fall 2027. Teaching responsibilities will include a course at all levels of departmental curriculum, including but not limited to a general education course, a major’s course in population, conservation, or evolutionary genetics, and a graduate course in the candidate’s area of expertise. The development of an externally funded, collaborative research program involving undergraduate and graduate students is expected.  The candidate will also be expected to help academically advise biology students, supervise internships, serve on university committees, and participate in curriculum development as needed. The successful candidate will complement existing departmental strengths and address genetic/genomic research questions fundamental to population or evolutionary biology.  The candidate will have access to renovated teaching spaces for both didactic or active style instruction and can extend the classroom through research in recently remodeled laboratory spaces, a registered herbarium, a wildlife research lab, a prairie research plot, and the UCM Pertle Springs Wildlife and Recreation Area.  

Faculty within the College of Health, Science, and Technology at University of Central Missouri support the university’s mission of providing student-centered, quality education and are committed to the success of students.  This includes quality teaching, advising, collegiality and communication.  In addition, faculty provide service to their program, department and university, engage in research, scholarship, and professional development activities. Engaging in committee work that will advance the department/college/institution.

Participating in graduation and convocation ceremonies.

This implies an understanding of the communication hierarchy within departments, colleges, and administrative levels. Timely communication with students supports other faculty responsibilities (teaching, advising).

Be responsive and timely. Respond to student phone calls and email messages within university guidelines.

Postdoctoral experience.

Revitalizing Hunting, Fishing and Trapping in White Earth Using Participatory GIS

Project Summary
Hunting, fishing and trapping are essential components of the culture and livelihoods of tribal nations throughout Minnesota. However, participation in these activities have been steadily decreasing in many communities. This is concerning because wild meat and fish are critical to tribal protein sovereignty and security. The Umana Laboratory (PIs: Christopher Shaffer and Marissa Milstein) in the Department of Fisheries, Wildlife and Conservation at the University of Minnesota – Twin Cities is recruiting a Masters Student in the Conservation Sciences program for a participatory mapping project focused on revitalizing hunting, fishing and trapping in the White Earth Nation. This research is in partnership White Earth Natural Resources and seeks to 1) identify the barriers to participation in these activities and 2) develop a community-based GIS for education, traditional knowledge exchange and increasing management capacity.

Assessing the distribution of Cacao Mild Mosaic Virus (CaMMV) and its mealybug vectors across cacao-producing regions in Puerto Rico.
Evaluate the transmission dynamics of aphids and thrips and investigate their associations with CaMMV.
Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will receive hands-on research experience in plant pathology, entomology, and molecular biology. Training will include identification of mealybugs, aphids, and thrips using both taxonomic keys and molecular techniques; evaluation of CaMMV incidence in commercial cacao farms; and application of molecular methods to study virus–vector–host interactions. You will gain experience in DNA extractions, PCR amplification, and sequence analysis for both insect vectors and CaMMV as well as the use of laboratory equipment such as autoclave, sterilizers, centrifuges, and homogenizers.

MSc student – Marbled Murrelet at-sea population monitoring

Cal Poly Humboldt is searching for a graduate student (MSc) for a partially funded research project conducting at-sea population monitoring of threatened Marbled Murrelet (Brachyramphus marmoratus) and other seabirds in California and Oregon. This work is part of a long-term monitoring project mandated by the Northwest Forest Plan, and is in collaboration with Oregon State University. 

Organization: Department of Wildlife, Cal Poly Humboldt

Position description: The position will begin in May 2027. The successful candidate will participate in at-sea surveys for Marbled Murrelet and all other marine birds in near coastal areas throughout northern California and southern Oregon during the breeding season (~May 15 - July 31). The candidate will be mentored by Drs. Daniel Barton and Frank Fogarty (Cal Poly Humboldt), and Dr. Rachael Orben (Oregon State University). There is the opportunity to investigate research questions related to population trends for other species in a long-term data set. The successful candidate is also expected to participate in at-sea surveys throughout the Oregon coast in 2027, contingent on funding. The position includes field travel and housing, tuition, full-time summer salary and part-time academic year salary (~$20/hr), with the possibility of additional salary support from teaching assistant positions. 

Required qualifications:

·         BSc in biology, zoology, wildlife ecology, fisheries, or a related field

·         Strong oral and written communication skills

·         Ability to work both independently and as part of a team to achieve research goals

·         Willingness to travel and collect data in challenging conditions on small boats

·         Bird identification experience (especially PNW seabirds)

·         Interest in developing advanced quantitative skills 

·         The selected candidate will need to successfully apply to Cal Poly Humboldt’s Master of Science in Natural Resources program.

Preferred qualifications:

·         Experience using GIS and R to manage and analyze wildlife data
·         Experience collecting field data, including conducting point counts or other distance sampling methods
·         Familiarity with working on small boats in ocean conditions.

 

Interested candidates should submit the following to all three PIs ( [email removed], [email removed], [email removed] ) by Dec 1st for full consideration:

1.      A letter of research interests that includes relevant skills and experiences
2.      CV or resume, including contact information for at least two references
3.      Copy of unofficial transcripts

Job Description
Position Summary:
The Postdoctoral Researcher in Human–Wildlife Interactions will investigate how dynamic patterns of human activity shape wildlife behavior, habitat use, and landscape connectivity. The position offers an opportunity to integrate large human mobility datasets with ongoing and completed wildlife studies across the United States, linking fine-scale behavioral responses with broader patterns of habitat availability and connectivity. 

The Postdoctoral Researcher will work closely with Dr. Mark Ditmer (USFS Rocky Mountain Research Station & CSU); Dr. Philip Manlick (USFS Pacific Northwest Research Station), and Dr. George Wittemyer (CSU) to develop innovative approaches and questions involving the influence of human activities and disturbance.

Full Consideration Date: December 1, 2026

The Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Conservation Biology at Colorado State University seeks a highly motivated researcher with expertise in spatial ecology. Based within the Department of Fish, Wildlife, and Conservation Biology, this position will contribute to expanding the frontiers of knowledge through broad-based expertise in applied ecology, quantitative methods, and the human dimensions of fish and wildlife conservation and management.

The successful candidate will conduct independent and collaborative research focused on spatial ecology and the application of advanced analytical approaches to conservation and wildlife management challenges.

Essential Job Duties:
Conduct independent and collaborative research using spatial and spatiotemporal data to address conservation and wildlife management challenges.
Develop and apply quantitative methods and analytical approaches to ecological and conservation research.
Analyze, interpret, and communicate research findings through scientific publications, presentations, and technical reports.
Collaborate with interdisciplinary teams across ecology, conservation, natural resources, and related fields.
Contribute to the advancement of knowledge in applied ecology, quantitative methods, and the human dimensions of fish and wildlife conservation and management.

Conditions of Employment:
Must be legally authorized to work in the United States by the proposed start date. Colorado State University will not provide visa sponsorship for this position.
Must be able to work effectively both independently and as part of a collaborative research team.
Must be able to travel as required to conduct research and attend professional meetings.

Supervision:
May provide guidance, training, or mentoring to graduate students, undergraduate students, or research personnel associated with project activities.

Minimum Qualifications:
Ph.D. degree in a pertinent biological, physical, or computer science field.
Demonstrated research focus on spatial ecology.
Strong publication record in spatial ecology.
Experience with research design in field settings.

Preferred Qualifications:
Demonstrated proficiency in movement analyses, analysis of camera data, spatial statistical modeling, and/or processing of large datasets.
Demonstrated ability to develop and apply Geographic Information Systems (GIS) methods and tools.
Demonstrated proficiency with scientific computing and programming languages, such as MATLAB, R, Python, or similar languages used in research applications.
Research experience examining wildlife responses to human activity or environmental change.
Demonstrated experience working in collaborative research settings.
